title: Dihydropyridine CCB (amlodipine): peripheral edema
vignette: A 77-year-old man comes to the office after he was found to have high blood pressure during a health fair. His blood pressure is 158/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 74/min. Other physical examination findings are normal. The patient is started on a medication to treat his hypertension. During his follow-up visit 3 weeks later, he reports bilateral leg swelling. He has no chest pain, shortness of breath, or abdominal symptoms. His blood pressure is 135/65 mm Hg and pulse is 80/min. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal, but there is bilateral, symmetrical, 2+ pitting lower extremity edema. Laboratory studies show a serum creatinine level of 0.8 mg/dL, and urinalysis is negative for proteinuria. Which of the following was most likely prescribed to treat this patient's hypertension?

clues.text: started on a medication to treat his hypertension
clues.note: A new antihypertensive followed by a characteristic adverse effect is the setup - the side effect identifies the drug class.
Bilateral, symmetric lower-extremity edema shortly after starting an antihypertensive is the classic adverse effect of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers.
A normal heart/lung exam argues against heart failure as the cause of edema, pointing to a drug effect.
No proteinuria (and normal creatinine) excludes nephrotic syndrome/renal causes, supporting drug-induced peripheral edema.

whatMatters: New-onset bilateral peripheral edema after starting an antihypertensive, with a NORMAL heart/lungs, normal creatinine, and NO proteinuria = a DIHYDROPYRIDINE calcium channel blocker (AMLODIPINE). It preferentially dilates precapillary arterioles, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure and causing fluid extravasation (edema). Answer A.
strategy: Recognize the classic dihydropyridine-CCB adverse effect (peripheral edema) and exclude cardiac/renal causes (normal exam, creatinine, no proteinuria). Among the options, amlodipine is the dihydropyridine CCB. Reject drugs that REDUCE edema or don't cause it: ACE inhibitor (ramipril) / ARB (valsartan) balance arteriolar+venular dilation (reduce CCB edema; ramipril also causes cough), and diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, torsemide, eplerenone) decrease edema.

eliminations.label: Eplerenone - potassium-sparing diuretic (reduces edema)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (potassium-sparing diuretic). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: diuretics REDUCE fluid/edema; eplerenone wouldn't cause new peripheral edema (its risks are hyperkalemia). ✅ Correct if: resistant hypertension/heart failure needing aldosterone blockade.

eliminations.label: Hydrochlorothiazide - thiazide diuretic (reduces edema)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a thiazide diuretic increasing renal sodium excretion. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it decreases volume/edema; its adverse effects are hyponatremia/hypokalemia/hyperuricemia, not leg edema. ✅ Correct if: first-line HTN with electrolyte side effects.

eliminations.label: Ramipril - ACE inhibitor (balances dilation; cough)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an ACE inhibitor. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: ACE inhibitors dilate BOTH arterioles and venules, normalizing capillary pressure - they REDUCE (and are used to counter) dihydropyridine edema; their classic effect is cough/angioedema. ✅ Correct if: dry cough or angioedema.

eliminations.label: Torsemide - loop diuretic (reduces edema)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a loop diuretic for volume overload. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it reduces edema and is mainly used for volume overload, not routine HTN, and wouldn't cause leg edema. ✅ Correct if: managing volume overload.

eliminations.label: Valsartan - ARB (balances dilation)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an angiotensin receptor blocker. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: like ACE inhibitors, ARBs balance arteriolar/venular dilation and do not cause peripheral edema (they help offset CCB edema). ✅ Correct if: HTN needing RAAS blockade without cough.

reasoning: New antihypertensive -> bilateral peripheral edema with normal heart/lungs/kidney and no proteinuria
This is the signature adverse effect of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
Amlodipine is the dihydropyridine CCB among the options
mechanism: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, nifedipine) are effective first-line antihypertensives that act on vascular smooth muscle. They preferentially dilate PRECAPILLARY ARTERIOLES more than postcapillary venules, so more blood reaches the capillary bed while venous outflow resistance is relatively unchanged. This raises CAPILLARY HYDROSTATIC PRESSURE, driving fluid out of the capillaries into the interstitium and producing bilateral, symmetric, dependent PERIPHERAL EDEMA - not from fluid overload (the heart, kidneys, and albumin are normal, and there is no proteinuria). The edema is dose-related and can be reduced by adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB, which also dilate the venular side and normalize the transcapillary pressure gradient. Among the options, amlodipine is the dihydropyridine CCB; ACE inhibitors/ARBs (ramipril, valsartan) and diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, torsemide, eplerenone) do not cause - and generally reduce - peripheral edema.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Pharm > dihydropyridine CCBs (amlodipine, nifedipine): peripheral edema (precapillary arteriolar dilation -> ↑capillary hydrostatic pressure), flushing, reflex tachycardia; ACE/ARB reduce the edema.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Bilateral peripheral edema after a new antihypertensive, with normal heart/kidney = dihydropyridine CCB (amlodipine).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on dihydropyridine CCB, precapillary arteriole, capillary hydrostatic pressure, or peripheral vs cardiac edema? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Diuretics (HCTZ, torsemide, eplerenone) reduce edema; ACE inhibitor/ARB (ramipril, valsartan) balance dilation and offset CCB edema.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: dihydropyridine CCB -> peripheral edema (arteriolar > venular dilation); add ACE/ARB to reduce it.

keywords.back: Precapillary arteriolar dilation -> ↑capillary hydrostatic pressure -> fluid extravasation

keywords.front: How to reduce dihydropyridine CCB edema
keywords.back: Add an ACE inhibitor or ARB (balanced venular dilation)

firstAid.detail: Pharm: amlodipine -> peripheral edema (arteriolar dilation, ↑capillary pressure).
Pharm > ACE/ARB (cough/none, reduce edema), diuretics (reduce volume).
Pharm > add ACE inhibitor/ARB; dose-dependent, not diuretic-responsive.

memoryHook: Amlodipine opens the arteriole floodgates but not the venous drain - capillary pressure rises and ankles puff up; an ACE/ARB opens the drain to relieve it.
